articles.title: 5 .cursorrules Constraints That Instantly Stop AI Spaghetti Code in Cursor & Claude
articles.excerpt: When using AI coding assistants like Cursor or Claude Code on real production projects, generic prompts quickly lead to silent try/catch blocks, any type casts, and monolithic 300-line functions. Addi…
articles.body: When using AI coding assistants like Cursor or Claude Code on real production projects, generic prompts quickly lead to silent try/catch blocks, any type casts, and monolithic 300-line functions. Adding a strict .cursorrules file to your repository root turns the LLM from an unpredictable junior assistant into a disciplined senior engineer. 1. Ban Silent Catch Blocks LLMs love writing catch (err) { console.log(err); } so code compiles without crashing locally—which causes invisible data loss in production. - Never swallow exceptions silently. Always propagate typed errors or return explicit Result objects with actionable context. 2. Enforce Early Returns (Max Nesting: 2) Deep if/else pyramids make code brittle when AI edits a single branch. - Keep functions small and single-purpose.

articles.title: Switches in an EMC Test Setup: What Actually Breaks the Measurement
articles.excerpt: An EMC test setup is a measurement instrument built by hand. Antennas, cables, amplifiers, a receiver and — usually — one or more switches that let a single receiver look at several antennas or severa…
articles.body: An EMC test setup is a measurement instrument built by hand. Antennas, cables, amplifiers, a receiver and — usually — one or more switches that let a single receiver look at several antennas or several paths. The switch is the part of that instrument nobody calibrates properly, which is odd because it is the only part whose loss changes every time a relay closes. This note is about the specific ways switches degrade an EMC measurement, and what to specify so they do not. The path loss you calibrated is not the path loss you have Radiated emissions measurements are made by subtracting a substitution loss from a receiver reading. That loss is the sum of antenna factor, cable loss, amplifier gain and switch loss. The first three are stable.

articles.body: Every dB of loss placed between an antenna and a low-noise amplifier costs the same as a dB of noise figure, except you cannot buy your way out of it later with a better LNA. That single sentence explains most of the bad antenna-switching designs I have seen reviewed: the switch gets treated as plumbing, sized on power handling and connector type, and then the link budget quietly loses half a dB that nobody accounts for. Antenna switching is where receiver design is decided, not where it is implemented. The arithmetic that decides the part Cascaded noise figure for two stages is: F_total = F1 + (F2 - 1) / G1 A 0.5 dB insertion loss is F1 = 1.122 , G1 = 0.891 .

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?

articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.
